# Abstract

The Colonial Spanish Amazon (1.874.185 km², 22.139 active 5-arcminute terrestrial cells) comprised the vast eastern watershed of the Andes stretching from the headwaters of the Caquetá and Putumayo southwards across the Marañón, Huallaga and Ucayali basins to the seasonally inundated llanos of Moxos and the dry forest plateau of Chiquitos. Across nearly three centuries from Francisco de Orellana's descent of the Amazon in 1542AD to the close of the Spanish American wars of independence in 1825AD, this frontier was governed through missionary reductions, cordilleran garrison towns and fluvial outposts designed to secure the eastern flanks of the Viceroyalties of Peru and New Granada against indigenous resistance and Portuguese expansion. Reconstructed across eight benchmark horizons, regional population experienced a protracted post-contact collapse from 1.325.000 in 1542AD (70,7 persons per 100 km²) to 908.000 in 1600AD and 696.000 in 1650AD, falling to a demographic nadir of 467.000 in 1780AD (24,92 persons per 100 km²), before staging a modest recovery to 506.000 by 1825AD (27 persons per 100 km²).

Demographic trajectories diverged across four distinct administrative and physiographic divisions. In the Comandancia General de Maynas (687.680 km², 36,7% of regional area), population contracted from 510.000 in 1542AD to 155.000 in 1780AD before rebounding slightly to 170.000 in 1825AD (24,72 persons per 100 km²), driven by severe epidemic mortality along the mainstem várzea and the retreat of survivors into interfluvial terra firme refuges. In the Gobernación de Quijos, Canelos and Macas (110.538 km², 5,9%), population dropped from 185.000 in 1542AD to 52.000 in 1780AD and 58.000 in 1825AD (52,47 persons per 100 km²), reflecting brutal sixteenth-century encomienda exactions, the Jumandi revolt of 1578AD and persistent gold-washing mortality. Across the northern missions of Caquetá, Putumayo, Vaupés and Amazonas (414.281 km², 22,1%), population fell from 240.000 in 1542AD to 90.000 in 1780AD and 1825AD (21,72 persons per 100 km²). Conversely, in Moxos, Chiquitos and Santa Cruz de la Sierra (661.686 km², 35,3%), population dropped from 390.000 in 1542AD to 170.000 in 1780AD before expanding to 188.000 by 1825AD (28,41 persons per 100 km²), where extensive Jesuit cattle ranching and indigenous cotton manufacturing provided an economic foundation that buffered the region against post-expulsion decline.

The primary mechanism of depopulation was the introduction of lethal Old World pathogens, notably smallpox, measles, influenza and dysentery, which spread rapidly through nucleated mission settlements. This biological catastrophe was compounded by the disruption of traditional riverine subsistence, forced relocation into crowded reductions and aggressive slaving expeditions by Portuguese *bandeirantes* from São Paulo and *tropas de resgate* from Belém do Pará. To prevent double counting between nucleated mission populations and dispersed rural inhabitants, 188 catalogued colonial settlements are georeferenced and subtracted from sub-regional totals, yielding a consistent longitudinal reconstruction of colonial Amazonian demography.

# Background

## Physical Geography and Frontier Ecology

The Colonial Spanish Amazon occupied a vast transitional zone between the eastern cordilleras of the Andes and the lowland interior of the Amazon and La Plata drainage basins [@taylor1999western; @sweet1974rich]. Covering 1.874.185 km², the region encompassed three contrasting ecological domains: the steep, forested Andean piedmont (the Ceja de Selva or Montaña), the immense riverine floodplains (várzea) and forested interfluves (terra firme) of the Upper Amazon, and the open savanna wetlands and dry forests of eastern Bolivia [@block1994mission; @radding2005landscapes].

In the Upper Amazon, the Marañón, Huallaga, Ucayali and Napo rivers descend rapidly from the cordillera through turbulent gorges before meandering across the lowland plain [@vega1992estructura; @coomes2021geolocatio]. These blackwater and whitewater river systems supported dense pre-Columbian riverine societies described by Gaspar de Carvajal during Orellana's voyage in 1542AD [@sweet1974rich]. The seasonal flood pulse deposited fertile Andean silt along river banks, sustaining productive maize and manioc cultivation alongside rich aquatic fauna including pirarucu (paiche), manatees and river turtles [@kettle2026climate]. In contrast, the interfluvial terra firme soils were acidic and nutrient-poor, supporting lower human densities dependent on shifting swidden agriculture and hunting.

In the south, the Llanos de Moxos formed a seasonally flooded tropical savanna basin drained by the Mamoré, Beni and Guaporé rivers [@block1994mission; @paper2003waging]. During the rainy season from December to April, floodwaters submerged extensive areas, creating an aquatic landscape where pre-Columbian inhabitants had constructed vast networks of raised agricultural fields, forest islands, causeways and canals [@block1994mission; @rodriguez2014indigenous]. East of Moxos, the Chiquitano plateau comprised undulating granitic hills and dry deciduous forest connecting the Amazonian watershed with the Upper Paraguay basin [@radding2005landscapes; @lobo1960caminho]. This southern frontier enjoyed a drier, more seasonal climate than the equatorial rainforests to the north, facilitating the introduction of European cattle and horses during the seventeenth century [@block1994mission].

## Linguistic Diversity and Pre-Columbian Demography

Prior to European contact, the Upper Amazon and Eastern Lowlands hosted exceptional ethnolinguistic diversity [@taylor1999western; @reeve1993regional]. Major linguistic families intersected across complex riverine and terra firme mosaics:
1. Arawakan languages, represented by the Campa (Asháninka), Piro (Yine) and Machiguenga along the Ucayali and Urubamba piedmont, and by the Mojo and Baure throughout the savanna wetlands of the Mamoré basin [@block1994mission; @taylor1999western].
2. Tupí-Guaraní speech communities, including the riverine Omagua and Cocama along the mainstem Marañón and Amazon, and the Chiriguano (Ava Guaraní) along the Andean foothills south of Santa Cruz de la Sierra [@sweet1974rich; @lobo1960caminho].
3. Panoan groups, dominating the central Ucayali and Javari basins, including the Shipibo, Conibo, Cashibo and Mayoruna [@chaumeil1981historia].
4. Zaparoan and Jivaroan peoples, occupying the Pastaza, Morona and Upano river valleys between Maynas and Quijos [@taylor1999western; @reeve1993regional].
5. Tukanoan and Barbacoan languages, concentrated in the Putumayo, Caquetá and Napo headwaters, including the Siona, Secoya, Coreguaje and Cofán [@gomezgonzalez2014misiones].
6. Chiquito and isolated language isolates, forming a mosaic of sedentary farming communities across the granitic hills of eastern Santa Cruz [@radding2005landscapes; @kuhne2025churches].

Pre-contact population density mirrored these ecological and linguistic divisions. Fertile várzea levee settlements along the Amazon, Marañón and lower Napo sustained nucleated linear villages that chroniclers described as extending for leagues without interruption, achieving local densities of 150 to 250 persons per 100 km² [@sweet1974rich]. In the savannas of Moxos, hydraulic earthwork agriculture supported aggregate populations exceeding three hundred thousand inhabitants [@block1994mission]. In contrast, interfluvial terra firme forests maintained mobile hunting and swidden groups at densities rarely exceeding 15 to 30 persons per 100 km² [@taylor1999western].

Spanish control across this expansive frontier was fragmented and uneven, structured around four administrative jurisdictions (Table \ref{tab:subregions}):

### Comandancia General de Maynas (Peruvian Amazon)

The Comandancia General de Maynas encompassed the vast river basins of the Marañón, Huallaga, Ucayali, Pastaza and Napo (687.680 km², 36,7% of the regional area). Spanish penetration began from highland gateways at Chachapoyas (founded 1538AD) and Moyobamba (founded 1540AD) [@taylor1999western]. In 1638AD, Governor Pedro Vaca de la Cadena founded the garrison town of San Francisco de Borja near the Pongo de Manseriche, opening the region to the Society of Jesus [@vega1992estructura; @grohs1974reducciones].

Jesuit missionaries, initiated by Fathers Lucas de la Cueva and Raimundo de Santa Cruz, gathered diverse indigenous groups into riverine reductions, including Mainas, Jeberos, Cocamas, Omaguas and Yurimaguas [@vega1992estructura; @chaumeil1981historia]. The Bohemian Jesuit Father Samuel Fritz worked along the mainstem Amazon between 1686AD and 1723AD, establishing thirty-eight mission settlements from the Huallaga confluence down to the Rio Negro [@fritz1922journal; @sweet1974rich]. Fritz mapped the Amazon basin and actively defended indigenous neophytes against Luso-Brazilian slave raids [@fritz1922journal]. Following the expulsion of the Jesuits in 1767AD, administration passed to secular clergy and the Franciscan Colegio de Ocopa, until Governor Francisco Requena organised the frontier into the Comandancia General de Maynas in 1802AD, transferring jurisdiction from the Viceroyalty of New Granada to the Viceroyalty of Peru [@taylor1999western].

### Gobernación de Quijos, Canelos and Macas (Ecuadorian Oriente)

Directly east of Quito lay the Gobernación de Quijos, Canelos and Macas (110.538 km², 5,9%), the smallest but most densely populated frontier division [@newson1995life; @reeve1993regional]. Lured by indigenous reports of the *País de la Canela* (Cinnamon Country), Gonzalo Pizarro and Francisco de Orellana led a major expedition from Quito in 1541AD, culminating in Orellana's navigation of the Amazon to the Atlantic [@sweet1974rich].

In 1559AD, Gil Ramírez Dávalos founded Baeza, followed by Avila (1563AD) and Archidona (1580AD) [@newson1995life]. Spanish encomenderos imposed brutal labour demands, compelling indigenous Quijos to collect wild cinnamon, wash riverine gold and transport cargo over steep Andean trails [@newson1995life; @reeve1993regional]. This intense exploitation provoked the Jumandi uprising of 1578AD, in which indigenous warriors destroyed Avila and Archidona before being crushed by Spanish forces [@newson1995life]. Farther south, the settlement of Sevilla del Oro (Macas) founded in 1575AD suffered repeated attacks from Shuar (Jívaro) communities, who successfully resisted Spanish domination throughout the colonial era [@taylor1999western].

### Misiones de Caquetá, Putumayo, Vaupés and Amazonas (Colombia)

Covering 414.281 km² (22,1% of regional area), the northern frontier comprised the dense rainforest basins of the Caquetá (Japurá), Putumayo (Içá), Vaupés and Guaviare rivers [@gomezgonzalez2014misiones]. Penetration began from the cordilleran valley of Sibundoy and the piedmont garrison of Mocoa, founded in 1563AD [@gomezgonzalez2014misiones].

Franciscan friars from the Province of Santa Fe established custodial missions among Cofán, Siona-Secoya, Coreguaje and Witoto peoples [@gomezgonzalez2014misiones]. Navigational hazards, rapid river currents and fierce resistance from uncontacted groups severely restricted missionary expansion. Throughout the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, mission settlements in the Caquetá and Putumayo experienced high rates of abandonment and relocation, serving primarily as fragile buffer posts between the Viceroyalty of New Granada and Portuguese expeditions ascending the Japurá and Rio Negro [@gomezgonzalez2014misiones; @sweet1974rich].

### Moxos, Chiquitos and Santa Cruz de la Sierra (Bolivian Lowlands)

The southern division (661.686 km², 35,3%) encompassed the savanna floodplains of Moxos, the dry forests of Chiquitos and the secular agricultural district of Santa Cruz de la Sierra [@block1994mission; @radding2005landscapes]. Founded by Ñuflo de Chaves in 1561AD and relocated westward in 1592AD, Santa Cruz de la Sierra functioned as a military stronghold against hostile Guaraní-speaking Chiriguanos and a staging base for slaving expeditions into the interior [@block1994mission; @lobo1960caminho].

Jesuit evangelisation commenced in Moxos with the foundation of Nuestra Señora de Loreto in 1682AD and Santísima Trinidad in 1686AD by Fathers Pedro Marbán, Cipriano Barace and José Castillo [@block1994mission; @rodriguez2014indigenous; @paper2003waging]. Between 1682AD and 1744AD, the Jesuits gathered over thirty thousand Mojo, Baure, Canichana, Cayuvava, Movima and Itonama peoples into fifteen large mission towns [@block1994mission; @jackson2015demographic]. Simultaneously, Jesuit Father José de Arce established the Chiquitos missions beginning with San Francisco Javier in 1691AD, expanding to ten major reductions by 1755AD [@radding2005landscapes; @gangui2021orientatio; @kuhne2025churches]. Unlike the fragile Upper Amazon missions, Moxos and Chiquitos developed thriving agro-pastoral economies featuring tens of thousands of cattle, irrigated agriculture, weaving workshops, sophisticated musical ensembles and monumental carved-timber churches [@block1994mission; @nawrot2018indian; @nawrot2019musica; @trujillo2010arquitectu; @gangui2026todos].

# Methodology

## Frontier Demarcation and Benchmark Cadence

Regional demography is tracked across eight benchmark dates: 1542AD, 1600AD, 1650AD, 1700AD, 1750AD, 1780AD, 1800AD and 1825AD. The opening benchmark captures the immediate contact baseline established by Orellana's initial descent, prior to widespread epidemic diffusion into the interior. The centennial horizons (1600AD, 1650AD, 1700AD, 1750AD) document the expansion of the Jesuit and Franciscan reduction systems. The 1780AD horizon marks the post-expulsion crisis and demographic trough, while 1800AD and 1825AD track late colonial recovery up to the independence era.

Data sources incorporate ecclesiastical mission censuses (*padrones*), baptismal and burial registers, Jesuit annual reports (*cartas anuas*), administrative inspections (*visitas*) and reports by colonial governors [@block1994mission; @newson1995life; @newson2020cultural; @grohs1974reducciones; @gomezgonzalez2014misiones]. Because colonial counts often recorded only tributary males or baptised families (*neófitos*), standard multipliers (3,8 to 4,5 persons per tributary family) are applied to reconstruct total populations [@newson1995life; @jackson2015demographic]. To reflect uncertainty in historical reporting and uncontacted populations (*infieles* or *monteses*), explicit symmetric uncertainty intervals (+/- 14% to 16%) are maintained across all sub-regions (Table \ref{tab:bounds}).

## Historical Cadastres and Census Enumeration

Colonial statistical records for the Spanish Amazon survive across diverse archival series [@block1994mission; @newson1995life; @taylor1999western]:
1. The 1577AD and 1582AD *Relaciones Geográficas de Indias*, providing early counts of tributary repartimientos in Baeza, Avila and Archidona [@newson1995life].
2. Jesuit missionary reports, notably Father Francisco de Figueroa's 1661AD relation of the Maynas missions and Father Manuel Rodríguez's 1684AD chronicle *El Marañón y Amazonas* [@grohs1974reducciones; @vega1992estructura].
3. The cartographic and census logs of Father Samuel Fritz (1689AD to 1711AD), detailing neophyte counts across thirty-eight Omagua, Yurimagua and Ibanoma villages along the Amazon mainstem [@fritz1922journal].
4. The 1743AD Jesuit general catalogue of the Maynas missions, recording 11.234 neophytes across twenty-two active reductions [@grohs1974reducciones].
5. The 1767AD expulsion inventories (*inventarios de temporalidades*), providing comprehensive enumerations for Moxos (32.227 inhabitants across fifteen reductions) and Chiquitos (23.788 inhabitants across ten reductions) [@block1994mission; @jackson2015demographic].
6. Governor Francisco Requena's 1785AD inspection of Maynas and Francisco de Viedma's 1788AD description of the Province of Santa Cruz de la Sierra [@taylor1999western; @block1994mission].
7. The 1796AD episcopal inspection by Bishop José Sánchez Rangel and the 1810AD-1825AD late colonial provincial censuses compiled prior to republican reorganization [@taylor1999western].

## Epidemiological Waves and Depopulation Ratios

Depopulation across the Spanish Amazon followed a devastating non-linear trajectory driven by recurrent epidemic waves [@newson1996epidemics; @sweet1974rich]. Unlike Andean highland communities where depopulation ratios typically reached 4:1 or 5:1, lowland Amazonian populations suffered catastrophic disruption due to immunological vulnerability and communal living arrangements in thatched communal longhouses (*malocas*) [@taylor1999western; @sweet1974rich].

Major documented epidemic outbreaks included:
1. The pandemic of 1589AD: Smallpox and measles swept through Quito and the Quijos piedmont, halving native populations in Baeza and Archidona within two years [@newson1995life].
2. The Marañón epidemics of 1660AD and 1669AD: Smallpox devastated the early Maynas reductions, carrying off over twenty thousand Mainas and Jeberos and triggering the abandonment of Borja [@grohs1974reducciones; @vega1992estructura].
3. The Amazon pandemic of 1680AD to 1691AD: Introduced via Belém and Portuguese slaving canoes, smallpox decimated the Omagua and Yurimagua towns mapped by Fritz, reducing settlements that had numbered several thousand inhabitants to scattered remnants [@fritz1922journal; @sweet1974rich].
4. The Moxos epidemics of 1728AD, 1749AD and 1764AD: Smallpox and measles repeatedly struck the Mamoré reductions, causing mortality spikes of 25% to 40% in Loreto, Trinidad and San Ignacio [@block1994mission; @jackson2015demographic].

Mission reductions exacerbated epidemic mortality by gathering dispersed, mobile family bands into dense, permanent settlements with poor sanitation [@block1994mission; @jackson2015demographic]. When epidemics broke out, indigenous neophytes frequently fled into the forest, carrying contagion to uncontacted groups across the interfluves [@chaumeil1981historia].

## Luso-Brazilian Encroachment and Frontier Demarcation

The demographic trajectory of the Spanish Amazon was intimately tied to geopolitical conflict with Portuguese Brazil [@hemming1978red; @sweet1974rich]. Under the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494), Spanish sovereignty theoretically extended eastward to the mouth of the Amazon. In practice, Portuguese expansion from Belém do Pará after 1616AD steadily pushed the effective border thousands of kilometres westward up the Amazon, Madeira, Rio Negro and Guaporé rivers [@hemming1978red].

In the seventeenth century, São Paulo *bandeirantes* undertook long-distance slave-hunting expeditions into Spanish mission territories [@hemming1978red]. Between 1648AD and 1652AD, the massive expedition of Antônio Raposo Tavares crossed the Chaco, ravaged the Franciscan and Jesuit reductions of Moxos, descended the Mamoré and Madeira rivers, and reached Belém, capturing thousands of indigenous captives [@hemming1978red; @block1994mission]. Along the Amazon mainstem, official Portuguese *tropas de resgate* (ransom troops) ascended the river under the pretext of ransoming indigenous captives from hostile tribes, capturing entire villages of Omaguas, Yurimaguas and Mayorunas under Father Fritz's pastoral care [@fritz1922journal; @sweet1974rich].

The Treaty of Madrid (1750) and Treaty of San Ildefonso (1777) recognised Portuguese *uti possidetis*, formally ceding extensive Amazonian territories to the Portuguese Crown [@hemming1978red; @lobo1960caminho]. To reinforce the Guaporé frontier, the Portuguese constructed the massive stone fortress of Forte Príncipe da Beira (1776AD) directly opposite the Jesuit missions of Moxos, cementing Portuguese control over the eastern bank of the Iténez-Guaporé and driving Spanish reductions further west into the interior [@block1994mission].

## Settlement Subtraction and Rural Density Modelling

To prevent spatial double counting between nucleated colonial settlements and dispersed rural populations, 188 catalogued settlements are georeferenced within the four sub-regional masks. At each benchmark year, the active population of all catalogued settlements within a sub-region is summed and subtracted from the sub-regional total:

$$P_{\text{rural}}(t) = P_{\text{total}}(t) - \sum_{i=1}^{N_{\text{sett}}} P_i(t)$$

The residual rural population $P_{\text{rural}}(t)$ is allocated across non-settled 5-arcminute raster cells in proportion to biophysical habitability weights derived from riverine proximity, elevation, slope and vegetation cover [@kettle2026climate; @coomes2021geolocatio]. A two-dimensional smoothing filter applied across sub-regional boundaries ensures continuous spatial transitions without artificial border cliffs.

# Testing and Validation

Three primary validation criteria govern the demographic reconstruction of the Colonial Spanish Amazon:

1. **Source Ledger Reconciliation**: All 188 catalogued settlement records reconcile completely against the 240 candidate entries in the source ledger. The 52 excluded candidate records represent verified duplicate aliases and mission relocation records, yielding 0 unaccounted entries. Sub-regional coverage spans all four frontier divisions: 66 settlements in Maynas, 19 in Quijos, 34 in Caquetá-Putumayo and 69 in Moxos-Chiquitos.
2. **Spatial Bounding Box Integrity**: All 188 settlements possess verified WGS84 coordinates that fall strictly within their designated sub-regional envelopes, spanning from 20,46 S to 4,04 N latitude and 79,46 W to 57,46 W longitude.
3. **Trajectory and Hierarchy Consistency**: Population trajectories across all benchmark years adhere strictly to documented regional censuses and archival bounds. Figure \ref{fig:trajectory} confirms the regional population trajectory alongside the urban hierarchy of leading colonial centres.

# Results

## Chronological Trajectory of Frontier Demography

The demographic history of the Colonial Spanish Amazon divides into four broad chronological phases between 1542AD and 1825AD:

### Incursion, Encomienda and Initial Shock (1542AD to 1600AD)

In 1542AD, the regional indigenous population stood at approximately 1.325.000, supported by extensive flood-recession agriculture, productive fisheries and terra firme horticulture [@taylor1999western; @sweet1974rich]. By 1600AD, regional population had fallen by 31,5% to 908.000.

The sharpest proportional declines occurred in the Andean piedmont of Quijos and Maynas. In Quijos, where Spanish encomenderos subjected the native Quijos-Quichua to brutal labour regimes in gold washing and portage, population plummeted from 185.000 in 1542AD to 118.000 in 1600AD (a 36,2% loss) [@newson1995life]. The Jumandi rebellion of 1578AD devastated Spanish settlements but brought harsh military retaliation, followed by the deadly 1589AD smallpox epidemic that wiped out entire villages [@newson1995life]. In Maynas, population fell from 510.000 to 340.000 as early Spanish expeditions introduced respiratory infections and dysentery along the Marañón headwaters [@grohs1974reducciones].

### Jesuit Expansion and Fluvial Reductions (1600AD to 1700AD)

Between 1600AD and 1700AD, regional population dropped from 908.000 to 560.000, an additional 38,3% reduction. This century witnessed the rapid expansion of the Jesuit mission network in Maynas and Moxos [@block1994mission; @vega1992estructura].

While Jesuit reductions offered protection against Spanish encomenderos and Portuguese slavers, the congregation of immunologically virgin populations into permanent riverine villages created ideal conditions for epidemic diffusion [@jackson2015demographic]. In Maynas, successive waves of smallpox and measles in the 1660s and 1680s halved the population of the Maina and Jebero reductions, carrying total sub-regional population down from 340.000 in 1600AD to 195.000 in 1700AD [@grohs1974reducciones; @fritz1922journal]. In Moxos, where missionary reductions began in 1682AD, population fell from 275.000 in 1600AD to 185.000 in 1700AD, heavily impacted by the destructive slaving raid of Raposo Tavares in 1648-1652AD and subsequent virgin-soil epidemics [@block1994mission; @hemming1978red].

### Imperial Contestation, Expulsion and the Demographic Nadir (1700AD to 1780AD)

The eighteenth century brought increasing geopolitical tension between Spain and Portugal, culminated by the expulsion of the Jesuits in 1767AD. Total regional population reached its historical nadir of 467.000 in 1780AD, representing just 35,2% of the contact baseline.

The expulsion of the Society of Jesus in 1767AD destabilised frontier society [@block1994mission; @radding2005landscapes]. In Maynas, secular priests and military governors lacked the linguistic skills and organizational cohesion of the Jesuits; mission discipline disintegrated, agricultural production collapsed, and many indigenous neophytes abandoned the reductions to return to the interfluvial forests [@taylor1999western; @chaumeil1981historia]. In Moxos, secular administrators (*gobernadores*) instituted harsh commercial monopolies, extracting cacao, cotton cloth and tallow while neglecting church maintenance and food security [@block1994mission]. Severe epidemic outbreaks in 1764AD and 1785AD struck a vulnerable population, depressing sub-regional totals to 170.000 in Moxos-Chiquitos and 155.000 in Maynas by 1780AD [@block1994mission; @jackson2015demographic].

### Late Colonial Reorganization and Demographic Rebound (1780AD to 1825AD)

Between 1780AD and 1825AD, the regional population experienced a modest recovery, rising from 467.000 to 506.000 (an 8,4% expansion).

In Maynas, the administrative reforms of Governor Francisco Requena culminated in the Royal Cédula of 1802AD, which established the Comandancia General de Maynas under the Viceroyalty of Peru and brought Franciscan missionaries from Ocopa to re-establish frontier posts [@taylor1999western]. In Moxos and Chiquitos, indigenous *cabildos* (municipal councils) retained considerable autonomy, preserving their communal agricultural and cattle-herding institutions despite corrupt secular governors [@block1994mission; @radding2005landscapes]. Population in Moxos-Chiquitos rebounded from 170.000 in 1780AD to 188.000 by 1825AD, bolstered by significant secular population growth in Santa Cruz de la Sierra (reaching 13,4k by 1825AD) and Vallegrande (5,2k) [@block1994mission].

### Comandancia General de Maynas

Maynas exhibited the most severe geographic displacement of any frontier division [@taylor1999western; @grohs1974reducciones]. Pre-Columbian riparian populations along the Marañón and Amazon mainstems were virtually eliminated during the seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries [@fritz1922journal; @sweet1974rich]. The large, dense Omagua towns described by early chroniclers, which stretched along hundreds of kilometres of river islands, disappeared as survivors succumbed to smallpox or were captured by Portuguese slave raiders [@fritz1922journal; @hemming1978red].

In their place, the Jesuit missions created ethnically mixed reductions along tributary rivers such as the Huallaga, Ucayali and Pastaza [@vega1992estructura; @chaumeil1981historia]. Jeberos (founded 1640AD) on the Aipena river grew to 4,1k peak, functioning as the primary Jesuit administrative capital in the interior [@vega1992estructura]. Lagunas (Santiago de la Laguna, founded 1670AD) near the Huallaga mouth anchored Cocama populations (3,8k peak). However, frequent epidemic outbreaks and indigenous revolts caused constant instability. By 1825AD, highland gateway cities such as Chachapoyas (5,5k in 1825AD, 16,6k peak) and Moyobamba (5,1k in 1825AD, 15,3k peak) accounted for a large proportion of the sub-region's nucleated population, while the lowland interior remained sparsely settled [@taylor1999western].

### Gobernación de Quijos, Canelos and Macas

In Quijos, colonial exploitation transformed a dense indigenous chiefdom into a fragmented, depopulated borderland [@newson1995life; @reeve1993regional]. Following the failure of the 1578AD Jumandi uprising and the 1589AD smallpox epidemic, native Quijos adopted Quechua as a lingua franca, coalescing into the Quijos-Quichua (Yumbo) ethnic identity [@reeve1993regional]. Spanish towns such as Baeza, Archidona and Avila shrank into modest hamlets where a handful of Spanish families dominated indebted native peons [@newson1995life].

In the southern sector, the Canelos mission along the Bobonaza river maintained fragile Dominican posts among Zaparoan and Achuar groups [@taylor1999western]. In Macas, Spanish settlers engaged in small-scale gold washing along the Upano river, living in constant apprehension of Shuar raids [@taylor1999western]. Sub-regional population remained suppressed between 52.000 and 58.000 throughout the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries.

### Misiones de Caquetá and Putumayo

The northern frontier remained the most isolated and sparsely populated domain of the Spanish Amazon [@gomezgonzalez2014misiones]. Franciscan missions relied on indigenous labour in the Sibundoy valley to maintain mountain trails connecting Pasto and Popayán with the Amazonian lowlands [@gomezgonzalez2014misiones].

Mocoa (founded 1563AD) served as a precarious administrative outpost at the foot of the cordillera (4,2k peak), while riverine missions along the Putumayo and Caquetá faced continuous disruption from tropical fevers, flooded trails and native resistance [@gomezgonzalez2014misiones]. Portuguese slaving expeditions ascending the Japurá (Caquetá) routinely carried off indigenous neophytes, forcing Franciscan friars to abandon downriver reductions and pull missions back toward the Andean foothills [@gomezgonzalez2014misiones; @sweet1974rich]. Consequently, the sub-region's population stagnated at approximately 90.000 from 1780AD to 1825AD.

### Moxos, Chiquitos and Santa Cruz de la Sierra

In marked contrast to the Upper Amazon, Moxos and Chiquitos demonstrated extraordinary institutional resilience [@block1994mission; @radding2005landscapes]. Under Jesuit direction, indigenous Mojo and Chiquitano populations constructed ten to fifteen large, geometrically planned towns centred on monumental timber churches [@trujillo2010arquitectu; @gangui2021orientatio; @kuhne2025churches].

Towns such as Santísima Trinidad (4,9k peak), San Ignacio de Moxos (4,2k peak), San Ignacio de Velasco (4,1k peak), San José de Chiquitos (3,9k peak) and Concepción (3,8k peak) maintained thriving cottage industries producing fine cotton textiles, carved woodwork, silverwork and musical instruments [@block1994mission; @nawrot2016musical; @nawrot2018indian; @rodriguez2014indigenous]. Extensive cattle herds roaming the Moxos savannas numbered over fifty thousand head by 1767AD, providing an abundant meat supply that protected indigenous populations from seasonal famine [@block1994mission]. Even after the Jesuit expulsion, indigenous *cabildos* maintained communal town governance, musical performance and cattle ranching, buffering the region against severe depopulation and supporting a robust recovery to 188.000 inhabitants by 1825AD [@block1994mission; @radding2005landscapes].

## Interfluvial Refuges and Demographic Resistance

Throughout the colonial period, unreduced indigenous groups utilized the immense interfluvial terra firme forests as defensive refuges against colonial reduction and slave raiding [@taylor1999western; @chaumeil1981historia]. Communities such as the Waorani (Auca), Mayoruna (Matsés), Cashibo and independent Shuar abandoned major river corridors, retreating into headwater streams inaccessible to colonial canoes [@taylor1999western].

These refuge communities adopted highly mobile subsistence strategies, dispersing into small family units, shifting residential hamlets frequently and cultivating concealed manioc gardens hidden beneath the forest canopy [@chaumeil1981historia]. By avoiding riverine mission nucleations, these groups escaped the direct impact of mission epidemics, maintaining viable populations that persisted beyond the reach of colonial tribute registers [@taylor1999western]. Their demographic survival accounts for the substantial residual rural population that persisted across Maynas and Caquetá even at the height of colonial depopulation.

## Agro-Pastoral Economies and Subsistence Stability

The contrasting demographic trajectories of the northern rainforest missions and southern savanna reductions stemmed fundamentally from their underlying subsistence regimes [@block1994mission; @radding2005landscapes]. In Moxos and Chiquitos, the Jesuits established a diversified agro-pastoral economy that integrated indigenous horticultural knowledge with European cattle raising, irrigated rice cultivation, cotton farming and sugar processing [@block1994mission]. By 1767AD, the cattle herds of Moxos exceeded fifty thousand head, supplying neophyte families with regular beef rations and tallow for domestic illumination [@block1994mission; @jackson2015demographic]. This dependable protein supply mitigated infant malnutrition and stabilized crude birth rates, enabling Mojo and Chiquitano populations to recover rapidly between epidemic outbreaks [@jackson2015demographic].

In sharp contrast, the Jesuit missions of Maynas and Franciscan missions of Caquetá-Putumayo lacked open pastures and remained tethered to fragile riverine subsistence [@grohs1974reducciones; @gomezgonzalez2014misiones]. Dependent on seasonal river turtle harvesting, manatee hunting and flood-recession manioc cultivation, northern mission populations were vulnerable to river level fluctuations and seasonal protein shortages [@kettle2026climate]. When unseasonable floods destroyed floodplain crops or washed away turtle egg banks, mission residents experienced acute subsistence crises that elevated infant mortality and accelerated flight into the forest [@sweet1974rich].
